nameStory: Viburnum venosum gets its species name 'venosum' from the Latin word for 'veiny,' referring to the prominent veins that run through its leaves like highways on a map. This distinctive vein pattern makes the leaves look almost embossed, as if nature drew the veins with a raised pen. The common name varies, but it's sometimes called veiny viburnum for this very feature.
description: Veiny viburnum is a medium-sized deciduous shrub that typically grows 4-8 feet tall with an upright, somewhat open branching pattern. Like other viburnums, it produces clusters of small white flowers in late spring, followed by dark berries in fall. The most striking feature is its leaves, which display unusually prominent veining that creates a textured, almost quilted appearance. This shrub has the classic viburnum look but with leaves that seem to tell their own story through their bold vein patterns.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval to egg-shaped leaves with exceptionally prominent veins that feel raised to the touch, creating a textured surface like fine embossed paper. The veins are so pronounced they're visible from several feet away.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flat-topped clusters of small, creamy-white flowers in late spring, each tiny bloom about 1/4 inch across with five petals. The flower clusters are 2-4 inches wide and have a sweet, light fragrance.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small berries that start red in late summer and ripen to dark blue or black in fall. The berries are about 1/4 inch long and have a slightly bitter taste.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright shrub with somewhat arching branches that create an open, vase-like shape. The bark on older stems is grayish-brown with shallow furrows.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Winter buds are reddish-brown and pointed, arranged in opposite pairs along the stems. The buds have a slightly fuzzy texture and no scales covering them.

habitat: **[UNCERTAIN]** Based on related viburnums, likely found in partially shaded woodlands, forest edges, and stream banks with moist, well-drained soil. May prefer slightly acidic conditions typical of New England's mixed deciduous and coniferous forests. Could also occur in woodland clearings and along hiking trails where there's dappled sunlight.

seasonality.spring: **[UNCERTAIN]** New leaves emerge with their characteristic prominent veining already visible, and clusters of fragrant white flowers appear in late spring, typically May to early June.
seasonality.summer: The distinctive veined leaves are at their most prominent, making this the best time for identification. Flowers fade and small green berries begin forming.
seasonality.fall: Berries ripen to dark blue-black and leaves may turn yellow or reddish before dropping, leaving the prominent vein pattern visible until leaf fall.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show opposite branching pattern and pointed, reddish-brown buds. Any persistent berries may remain and help with identification.

funFact: **[UNCERTAIN]** The veins on this viburnum's leaves are so prominent that you can actually feel them as raised ridges when you run your finger across the leaf surface - it's like reading botanical braille! This unusual texture makes it one of the most tactilely distinctive shrubs in New England forests.
confusionNotes: **[UNCERTAIN]** Most likely confused with other viburnums, but the exceptionally prominent leaf veining should distinguish it from relatives like mapleleaf viburnum or arrowwoods. Remember: if you can feel the veins like raised highways on the leaf surface, you're probably looking at veiny viburnum.
contextualKnowledge: **[UNCERTAIN]** With only 24 recorded observations in New England, this appears to be either a very rare native species or possibly a less common cultivated variety that occasionally naturalizes. The low observation count suggests it's not widely established in the region.
compareHints: **[UNCERTAIN]** Unlike the more common mapleleaf viburnum with its maple-shaped leaves or the arrowwoods with their toothed oval leaves, veiny viburnum's leaves are distinguished primarily by their extraordinarily prominent venation rather than their overall shape. While other viburnums may have visible veins, none have the raised, tactile vein pattern that makes this species unique. The leaf shape is more similar to nannyberry, but the textured surface sets it apart immediately.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's viburnums, hobblebush is easily distinguished by its large heart-shaped leaves and drooping, rooting branches - most other viburnums grow more upright.
Among New England's viburnums, mapleleaf viburnum is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves - all other viburnums have simple oval or toothed leaves.
Among New England viburnums, northern wild raisin's thick, leathery leaves with smooth edges make it distinctive.
Unlike other viburnums in New England, guelder-rose is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves.
Among New England's viburnums, nannyberry stands out for its tree-like size and glossy leaves with fine teeth all around the edges.
Unlike hobblebush with its large heart-shaped leaves or mapleleaf viburnum with maple-like foliage, southern arrowwood has distinctly toothed, oval leaves with straight parallel veins.
Among the viburnums, northern arrowwood is distinguished by its combination of coarsely toothed leaves, smooth leaf surfaces, and preference for wet areas.

Unlike our native viburnums, Japanese snowball produces those distinctive perfectly round, sterile flower clusters rather than the flat-topped fertile flower clusters of species like nannyberry or arrowwood.

Among New England's viburnums, linden viburnum is most easily distinguished by its heart-shaped leaves - most other viburnums have either lobed leaves (like mapleleaf viburnum), elongated leaves (like nannyberry), or toothed oval leaves (like the arrowwoods).
Wright viburnum differs from native viburnums like arrowwoods and wild raisins by its more pronounced leaf venation and the distinctive red-to-black berry color change.
Siebold's viburnum stands out from other viburnums by its distinctively large, deeply ribbed leaves with parallel veining - most other viburnums have smaller leaves or different vein patterns.
Among New England's viburnums, squashberry is unique for its three-lobed, maple-like leaves - most other viburnums have either simple oval leaves (like nannyberry) or more complex tooth patterns.
Among the arrowwoods, downy arrowwood is distinguished by its fuzzy leaf undersides and earlier bloom time compared to southern arrowwood, which has broader leaves and longer leaf stems.
Among New England's viburnums, blackhaw stands out for its particularly hard wood and oval berries - most other viburnums have round berries.

Tea viburnum differs from other New England viburnums by its oval berries that turn from red to black, rather than the round berries that stay red, blue, or black found in species like guelder-rose or arrowwoods.
Unlike native New England viburnums such as hobblebush or arrowwoods, wayfaring-tree has distinctly wrinkled, velvety leaves rather than smooth ones.
Among New England viburnums, Korean spice viburnum stands out for its incredible fragrance and compact size.
Among the viburnums, southern wild raisin stands out for its completely smooth leaf edges - most other viburnums have toothed leaves.
Unlike native New England viburnums which are all deciduous, leatherleaf viburnum keeps its leaves year-round.
